articles.title: The RBA isn't trying to stop inflation. So don't expect prices to fall - ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation
articles.summary: The RBA isn't trying to stop inflation. So don't expect prices to fall  ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation

source_detail.name: ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation

articles.full_text:
What is the Reserve Bank trying to achieve by raising interest rates?
In recent days, a video has done the rounds on social media of someone asking for help to understand what the RBA is up to. This is an edited version of what they said:
"If inflation means that prices are higher, does the RBA expect businesses to start reducing prices to make inflation decrease?
"Because I don't see businesses ever reducing prices. I've never seen a company say that they'll permanently reduce their prices.
"So how does inflation actually get fixed?"
It was a great question, but a little confusing. So let's untangle it and answer it.
Inflation is baked into the system
Many people may not know this, but the RBA actually wants consumer prices to rise by 2.5 per cent every year.
Loading...
That's what the RBA's "inflation target" is.
So if prices are rising by more than 2.5 per cent, the RBA tries to slow the pace at which prices are rising.
If prices are rising by less than 2.5 per cent, the RBA tries to get them to rise a bit faster.
The RBA does not want zero inflation. It wants prices to rise by 2.5 per cent every year on average.
What does that mean in reality? It means that once prices rise, they're not coming down.
If prices rise by 2.5 per cent this year, by 2.5 per cent next year, and by 2.5 per cent the following year, prices will clearly be higher after three years, right?
That's the dynamic that slowly pushes prices higher over time. Inflation is built into our system.
It explains why we all feel like we're in a rat race, why we're always chasing wage increases to keep up with constantly rising prices.
Prices rise at different rates over time
The Bureau of Statistics could help people to understand this phenomenon much better if it presented inflation graphically in a more intuitive way.
It should present inflation in a graph like this, because the blue line shows what actually happens to prices over time:
And it reflects how the human brain thinks about inflation.
In Australia, consumer prices are always rising when the economy's growing, but sometimes prices rise at a faster pace, and sometimes they rise at a slower pace.
And the blue line in the graph captures that phenomenon too.
For example, when the blue line steps up sharply, that's a period when prices have risen quickly.
When the steps are smaller, that's a period when prices have risen slowly.
So, the graph makes intuitive sense. It shows how the general price level in Australia's economy is always rising over time, but that it rises in fits and starts.
Is this graph confusing?
But look at how the ABS presents inflation in graphical form on its website:
It requires people to think their way through multiple analytical steps without telling them how to do it.
For example, that ABS graph isn't telling you that prices are rising or falling, as you might assume.
It's telling you that prices have risen constantly in recent years, but sometimes they have risen at a faster rate (when the blue line goes up) and sometimes they have risen at a slower rate (when the line goes down).
If nobody told you that, you'd be forgiven for thinking that the falling line meant falling prices.
It's not very intuitive. One wouldn't be surprised if that graph was contributing to the public's confusion about inflation.
The large increase in prices in recent years
Another reason why the alternative graph is a good way to represent inflation is that it helps us to see how much prices have risen over a specific time period.
For example, when RBA governor Michele Bullock says consumer prices have risen by "20 to 25 per cent over the last few years", this is what she's talking about:
And we can use the graph to tell another intuitive story about inflation by zooming in for a granular look at the blue line.
When we do that, we can see how prices stepped sharply higher in 2022 and 2023 (when inflation got really bad a few years ago).
We can see how prices stepped up more slowly in 2024 (that's when inflation eased considerably, which led to the RBA cutting rates three times in 2025):
And we can see how prices stepped up noticeably again in late 2025 and into 2026 (which explains why the RBA has been lifting rates again this year).
How the RBA is trying to fix inflation
Which brings us back to the question at the top of this article.
The RBA isn't trying to compel businesses to cut their prices to bring inflation down. It's trying to engineer a situation in which businesses stop raising their prices so quickly.
That's it.
The RBA governor has acknowledged that consumer prices have risen more than 20 per cent in recent years and they won't be returning to their old, lower prices.
But she says she wants prices to rise much more slowly for a while.
That's how the RBA plans to "fix" inflation.
The graph below shows how consumer prices would have risen by 8.85 per cent in the last five years if they had kept rising at their 2014–2019 rate, but how they're currently 24 per cent higher.
That's what the RBA is talking about when it says the growth in consumer prices has to slow back down to a less disruptive pace.
Now, it knows it can't do anything to stop inflation hitting Australia from overseas (higher fuel prices due to war in the Middle East) and from climate-related shocks to food prices and insurance premiums.
But it's still lifting interest rates to make financial conditions a little bit tighter in Australia to slow economic activity a bit more and to increase unemployment a little bit more (yes, that's true) so local businesses can't lift prices by more than 2.5 per cent a year in the coming years.
It knows it's flirting with triggering a recession by doing so, but it thinks it's necessary.
And if the ABS published more intuitive graphs that showed how consumer prices were typically always rising when the economy's growing, it would help Australians better understand that inflation was ever-present.
It's the pace of inflation that concerns policymakers, not inflation itself.

articles.title: Cmos Camera Market Forecast to 2035: Automotive Safety Mandates and Industrial Vision to Drive Growth - IndexBox
articles.summary: Cmos Camera Market Forecast to 2035: Automotive Safety Mandates and Industrial Vision to Drive Growth  IndexBox
articles.full_text:
Sony Semiconductor Solutions
Dominant market share in image sensors
According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Cmos Camera market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture.
The global CMOS camera market is undergoing a structural transformation from a volume-driven consumer electronics model to an application-specific, qualification-intensive ecosystem. While smartphone demand remains the largest volume base, growth through 2035 will be increasingly shaped by automotive safety mandates, industrial automation, medical imaging, and smart infrastructure. These segments demand not only higher performance in low-light sensitivity, dynamic range, and global shutter capabilities but also stringent reliability, functional safety compliance, and multi-year design-in cycles.
Supply chain dynamics are bifurcating: leading players are vertically integrating wafer-level packaging, ISP tuning, and software stacks, while smaller suppliers focus on niche applications or regional channels. Pricing power is shifting from sensor die alone to the integrated solution stack, making BOM cost a poor proxy for total cost of ownership. Geographic roles are crystallizing, with design IP concentrated in North America, Europe, and parts of Asia; high-volume fabrication in Taiwan, South Korea, and China; and module integration clustered in lower-cost regions.
Regulatory frameworks, particularly in automotive and medical, are becoming de facto product requirements, adding non-recurring engineering costs and timeline overhead. The market is forecast to grow at a moderate CAGR through 2035, with the market index reaching new highs as demand diversifies beyond consumer electronics.
The baseline scenario for the CMOS camera market from 2026 to 2035 anticipates steady expansion, underpinned by the proliferation of vision systems across automotive, industrial, medical, and security applications. While smartphone camera module demand will remain the largest single volume driver, its growth rate will decelerate as handset shipments plateau and per-device sensor count stabilizes. Instead, incremental growth will come from advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS) and autonomous vehicles, where camera counts per vehicle are rising, and from factory automation, where machine vision enables quality inspection and robotic guidance.
The industrial and medical segments are expected to grow faster than the overall market, driven by needs for high-speed, high-resolution, and specialized imaging such as NIR and global shutter. Supply-side factors include capacity expansions in 300mm wafer fabrication and advanced packaging, which will improve cost structures but also intensify competition. Pricing pressure will persist in consumer segments, while specialized applications command premium margins. Geopolitical and trade tensions may affect supply chain configurations, encouraging regional diversification. The market index (2025=100) is projected to reach 145 by 2035, corresponding to a CAGR of 3.8%.
This outlook assumes no major global recession and continued technology adoption in key end-use sectors.
Consumer electronics remains the largest end-use sector for CMOS cameras, dominated by smartphones, tablets, laptops, and wearables. In smartphones, the trend is toward higher resolution, larger sensors, and advanced features like optical image stabilization and computational photography, but unit growth has plateaued as replacement cycles lengthen. The segment is characterized by intense price competition and rapid technology cycles. Through 2035, demand will be sustained by emerging markets where smartphone penetration is still rising, and by new device categories such as AR/VR headsets, smart home cameras, and drones.
However, the share of consumer electronics in total CMOS camera demand will gradually decline as automotive and industrial applications grow faster. Key demand indicators include global smartphone shipments, average camera count per device, and adoption of multi-camera systems. Major companies include Sony, Samsung, OmniVision, and GalaxyCore. Current trend: Moderate growth, driven by smartphone upgrades and new form factors.
Major trends: Increasing camera count per smartphone (triple, quad cameras), Shift to higher resolution sensors (48MP, 64MP, 108MP), Integration of AI processing for computational photography, Growth in AR/VR and wearable devices with cameras, and Rising demand for 3D sensing and depth cameras.
Representative participants: Sony Semiconductor Solutions, Samsung Electronics, OmniVision Technologies, GalaxyCore, and SK Hynix.
The automotive sector is the fastest-growing end-use market for CMOS cameras, propelled by regulatory mandates for advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS) such as automatic emergency braking, lane keeping, and rearview cameras. Modern vehicles increasingly feature multiple cameras for surround view, driver monitoring, and forward-facing sensing. The transition to autonomous driving will further increase camera content per vehicle, with some Level 3+ vehicles using over 10 cameras. Automotive CMOS cameras must meet stringent reliability and functional safety standards (e.g., AEC-Q100, ISO 26262), leading to long design-in cycles and high qualification costs.
Demand indicators include global vehicle production, ADAS penetration rates, and autonomous vehicle development. Key suppliers include Sony, ON Semiconductor, STMicroelectronics, and Panasonic. Current trend: Strong growth, driven by ADAS and autonomous driving mandates.
Major trends: Rising camera count per vehicle for ADAS and autonomous driving, Increasing resolution and dynamic range requirements, Adoption of global shutter sensors for in-cabin monitoring, Integration of image signal processing for real-time decision making, and Growth in electric vehicles with advanced sensor suites.
Representative participants: Sony Semiconductor Solutions, ON Semiconductor, STMicroelectronics, Panasonic Corporation, and OmniVision Technologies.
Industrial and machine vision applications are a key growth driver for CMOS cameras, as factories automate quality control, robotic guidance, and logistics. CMOS sensors are increasingly preferred over CCD due to higher speed, lower power, and cost advantages. The segment demands high-resolution, high-speed, and often specialized imaging such as near-infrared (NIR) for inspecting agricultural products or global shutter for moving objects. The rise of smart manufacturing and Industry 4.0 is accelerating adoption. Through 2035, demand will be further boosted by AI-enabled vision systems that can perform complex inspections. Demand indicators include industrial robot installations, manufacturing output, and investment in automation.
Major players include Teledyne, Cognex, Basler, and Sony. Current trend: Robust growth, supported by automation and quality inspection.
Major trends: Shift from CCD to CMOS in machine vision, Increasing use of 3D vision and depth sensing, Integration of AI and deep learning for defect detection, Growth in collaborative robots requiring vision, and Demand for high-speed and high-resolution sensors.
Representative participants: Teledyne Technologies, Cognex Corporation, Basler AG, Sony Semiconductor Solutions, and Omron Corporation.
Medical and scientific imaging represents a high-value, specialized segment for CMOS cameras. Applications include endoscopy, microscopy, ophthalmology, and DNA sequencing. CMOS sensors are replacing CCDs in many medical devices due to lower power, smaller size, and faster readout. The trend toward minimally invasive surgery is driving demand for high-definition, small-diameter camera modules. In scientific research, CMOS cameras are used in fluorescence microscopy and high-throughput screening. Regulatory approval (e.g., FDA) and biocompatibility requirements create high barriers to entry. Demand indicators include healthcare expenditure, surgical procedure volumes, and research funding.
Key suppliers include Hamamatsu, Sony, Canon, and Nikon. Current trend: Steady growth, driven by minimally invasive surgery and diagnostics.
Major trends: Miniaturization for endoscopic and catheter-based imaging, Higher resolution and color fidelity for diagnostics, Integration with AI for real-time analysis, Growth in point-of-care and portable imaging devices, and Increasing use in digital pathology and laboratory automation.
Representative participants: Hamamatsu Photonics, Sony Semiconductor Solutions, Canon Inc, Nikon Corporation, and Teledyne Technologies.
Security and surveillance is a mature but evolving market for CMOS cameras. Traditional analog systems are being replaced by IP cameras with higher resolution and network connectivity. The integration of AI for video analytics, such as facial recognition and behavior detection, is driving demand for more advanced sensors. Smart city projects and public safety initiatives are key growth drivers, particularly in Asia-Pacific and the Middle East. However, privacy concerns and regulations may restrain adoption in some regions. Demand indicators include government spending on security, urbanization rates, and crime rates. Major suppliers include Hikvision, Dahua, Axis Communications, and Bosch Security.
Current trend: Moderate growth, with increasing adoption of smart cameras.
Major trends: Shift from analog to IP cameras, Increasing resolution (4K, 8K) and low-light performance, Integration of AI and edge computing for analytics, Growth in smart city and safe city projects, and Rising demand for thermal and multi-sensor cameras.
Representative participants: Hikvision, Dahua Technology, Axis Communications, Bosch Security Systems, and Sony Semiconductor Solutions.

articles.title: Record imports push U.S. trade balance deep into the red in August - BNN Bloomberg
articles.summary: Record imports push U.S. trade balance deep into the red in August  BNN Bloomberg
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — The U.S. trade deficit widened more than expected in August as imports jumped to a record high against the backdrop of robust domestic demand, keeping trade on track to again subtract from economic growth in the third quarter.
The deterioration reported by the Commerce Department on Tuesday was despite President Donald Trump’s aggressive tariffs on imports, which he has argued are meant to shrink the trade gap. The nation posted record goods trade deficits with at least three countries, including Mexico.
Economists have long argued that the U.S. did not have the capacity to produce enough goods to meet its consumption needs.
“The administration’s trade policies have largely been a failure, trade tariffs have done nothing to reduce America’s reliance on the import of foreign-produced goods,” said Christopher Rupkey, chief economist at FWDBONDS. “The cost of American labor is simply too high to produce goods here cheap enough for consumers to even think about purchasing. Even if US manufacturers were willing, the factories could not be built here fast enough to produce the goods that consumers depend on.”
The trade shortfall increased 13.7 per cent to $105.6 billion, the largest since March 2025, the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Economic Analysis and Census Bureau said. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast the deficit would be $102.0 billion.
The trade deficit was at $79.8 billion when Trump was elected for a second term in November 2024. August’s deterioration was flagged by data last week that showed an import-driven surge in the goods trade deficit.
Domestic demand increased at its fastest pace in more than 3-1/2 years in the second quarter, reflecting robust consumer spending and business spending on equipment, mostly related to AI. The trend appears to have spilled over into the third quarter, with data last month showing strong consumer spending in August as well as orders and shipments of nondefense capital goods, excluding aircraft.
But businesses are relying on imports to meet demand. Imports increased 4.3 per cent to an all-time high of $420.8 billion in August. Goods imports jumped 5.3 per cent to $342.2 billion. They were boosted by a $9.1 billion increase in industrial supplies and materials, which include petroleum.
Crude oil imports rose $3.3 billion while nonmonetary gold increased $3.1 billion. Nonmonetary gold is excluded in the calculation of gross domestic product. Capital goods imports soared $6.2 billion to a record high $146.4 billion, driven by semiconductors and other industrial machinery. But imports of computer accessories decreased $1.6 billion.
TRADE SET TO WEIGH ON GDP GROWTH
Exports rose 1.4 per cent to $315.2 billion. Goods exports increased 2.2 per cent to $205.7 billion, reflecting a $6.3 billion rise in industrial supplies and materials, mostly nonmonetary gold, crude oil and fuel oil. Capital goods exports rose $1.3 billion, lifted by semiconductors and computers. But exports of civilian aircraft fell $1.0 billion.
Consumer goods exports dropped $2.2 billion, pulled down by a $2.4 billion decline in pharmaceutical preparations.
The goods trade deficit increased 10.3 per cent to $136.6 billion in August. When adjusted for inflation, it widened $8.7 billion, or 8.2 per cent, to $114.7 billion. Trade has subtracted from GDP for three straight quarters, and economists estimate it could cut as much as 2.5 percentage points from GDP in the third quarter.
Growth estimates for the July-September quarter are mostly above a 3.0 per cent annualized rate, with consumer spending expected to offset the drag from imports. The economy grew at a 2.2 per cent pace in the second quarter.
Services imports rose less than $0.1 billion to $78.5 billion in August, amid a small gain in transport. Charges for the use of intellectual property fell as did travel.
Exports of services also advanced by less than $0.1 billion to $109.5 billion. There were modest increases in charges for the use of intellectual property and other business services. Travel and financial services both declined.
The nation had record goods trade shortfalls with Mexico, Vietnam and Malaysia. It maintained deficits with Taiwan, China, the European Union, South Korea, Canada and India among other trade partners. It, however, posted a record goods trade surplus with Belgium, while maintaining surpluses with the Netherlands, South and Central America, the United Kingdom, Hong Kong, Brazil, Australia and Saudi Arabia.
(Reporting by Lucia Mutikani; Editing by Paul Simao and Andrea Ricci )

articles.title: DHL sees PH gaining from supply chain shakeup - Inquirer.net
articles.summary: DHL sees PH gaining from supply chain shakeup  Inquirer.net
articles.full_text:
MANILA, Philippines — The Philippines ranks among the Asia-Pacific countries that could benefit from rewiring traditional supply chain networks, particularly the ongoing “China+1” shift, according to global shipping and logistics company DHL.
DHL Express Asia-Pacific CEO Ken Lee said geopolitical tensions and companies’ efforts to build more resilient supply chains were increasingly reshaping trade flows within Asia, reducing dependence on any single country or region.
Part of that shift is the so-called “China+1” strategy, under which companies diversify their sourcing or manufacturing operations by adding another production base alongside China.
READ: DHL cues another 5.9% price hike in 2027
“Diversification — and I think you’ve probably heard some people say the China +1 strategy — in a way is moving and evolving the whole logistics trends,” Lee said at a media briefing on the sidelines of the 2026 DHL GoTrade Summit in Pasay.
The Philippines, in particular, is part of DHL’s “Geographical Tailwinds 20” or GT20 framework, which identifies economies expected to benefit from supply chain diversification and shifting global trade flows.
READ: DHL Express banks on SMEs to drive 2026 growth
The list includes the Philippines alongside Singapore, Indonesia, Vietnam, India and China in the Asia-Pacific region.
“We do see that these 22 countries that we have identified, of which the Philippines is one of them, will be a beneficiary of this supply chain diversification,” Lee said.
DHL Express Philippines managing director Nigel Lockett said shipment volumes to the United States and Canada remained strong, while the company was seeing a “marked increase” in both inbound and outbound intra-Asia-Pacific traffic.
Technology, data center logistics and new energy are among the sectors DHL sees driving further growth.
DHL currently moves more than 9,200 shipments daily for about 5,900 customers in the Philippines and estimates that it holds a 60-percent share of the local international express market. About 87 percent of its customers are micro, small, and medium enterprises.
The logistics giant is also keeping the door open to further investments as demand grows.
DHL already operates a facility in Clark and has recently invested in a new facility at the Ninoy Aquino International Airport. For now, Lockett said there are no plans to invest specifically in Clark International Airport.
That contrasts with rivals United Parcel Service Co. and Federal Express Corp., which are expanding directly at Clark International Airport.
UPS plans to open a new sorting facility that will serve as a hub for cargo arriving from regional gateways like Hong Kong. FedEx will begin building a 78,000-square-meter facility at Clark to increase daily flight frequencies from three to as many as 20.
Still, Lockett expressed confidence that DHL could retain its foothold in the Clark and Subic markets.
“We’ve got quite a handy market share up in the Clark and Subic area,” he said. “While we may invest in ground infrastructure, while we may invest in commercial people on the ground, and it may be a larger facility, we won’t be investing per se in Clark airport.” /pai

articles.full_text:
Hong Kong, Oct. 06, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Magic Empire Global Limited (NASDAQ: MEGL) ("MEGL" or the "Company") today announced a new strategic initiative to expand into international commodity trading and supply chain finance, building on its established financial services platform in Hong Kong. Going forward, the Company intends to develop its business around two core pillars: commodity trading, focusing on mineral and energy resources, and financial services, centered on supply chain finance.
The Company has established a wholly-owned subsidiary in Hong Kong, Lunar Haste International Trading Limited, through which it is developing an integrated business comprising two complementary segments:
Commodity Trading: cross-border trading of timber, mineral and coal products, initially focusing on hardwood logs and sawn timber, iron ore, thermal coal and metallurgical coal, supplied to buyers in the United States, Europe and the Asia-Pacific region.
Supply Chain Finance: financing solutions for upstream suppliers and downstream buyers in the commodity sector, which may include pre-export financing, inventory and warehouse receipt financing, receivables financing, and letter of credit facilitation and related arrangements. Such financing solutions will be provided, where required, through licensed entities or in cooperation with licensed financial institutions, subject to applicable laws and regulations.
The Company has established a mature partnership network and supply chain resources across North America, Europe and Africa, including relationships with producers, mine operators, timber mills and end buyers. These resources are expected to provide the Company with stable access to supply and diversified sourcing channels from the outset of its trading operations.
The expansion is further anchored by the extensive industry experience of the Company's management team, which has more than 30 years of experience in commodity trading and has held key management roles at a number of multinational commodity, mineral and energy trading companies.
The Company believes that combining physical trading with supply chain finance creates a mutually reinforcing model. Trading activities provide direct visibility into cargo flows, counterparty performance and collateral quality, which supports disciplined credit decisions, while financing capabilities strengthen relationships with suppliers and buyers and enhance the Company's trading competitiveness.
"Our management team has spent more than 30 years building relationships across global commodity supply chains, and we have established a mature partnership network spanning North America, Europe and Africa," said Mei Wang, CFO of MEGL. "By pairing that industry expertise with MEGL's financial services capabilities, we can offer our partners both reliable trading channels and tailored financing. Commodity trading and supply chain finance will be the two pillars of MEGL's growth going forward."
The Company has completed its first commodity trading transaction through Lunar Haste International Trading Limited in the fourth quarter of 2026.

articles.title: MaxLinear Introduces Topaz™, One of the Industry's Most Advanced AI-Ready PON HGU Chips for 10G and Beyond - AOL.com
articles.summary: MaxLinear Introduces Topaz™, One of the Industry's Most Advanced AI-Ready PON HGU Chips for 10G and Beyond  AOL.com
articles.full_text:
CARLSBAD, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Oct 6, 2026--
MaxLinear, Inc. (Nasdaq: MXL), a designer and manufacturer of high-speed, mixed-signal integrated circuits (ICs), today announced Topaz™, one of the industry’s most advanced PON Home Gateway Unit (HGU) SoC. Designed for 10G broadband deployments and future fiber architectures, Topaz combines fiber access, packet processing, AI/ML acceleration, post-quantum cryptography (PQC) readiness, and intelligent power management into a single, highly integrated SoC. Topaz is designed to minimize market trade-offs—reducing system complexity, lowering bill-of-materials (BOM) costs, and accelerating time-to-market for OEMs and operators worldwide.
This press release features multimedia. View the full release here: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261006568528/en/
MaxLinear Introduces Topaz, one of the Industry's Most Advanced AI-Ready PON HGU Chips for 10G and Beyond
Topaz is optimized for PON Fiber Gateways, Ethernet, and Fixed Wireless Access (FWA) deployments. It provides processing performance, memory bandwidth, and connectivity required for next-generation gateways, including Wi-Fi 8, and AI-enabled services, while enabling upgrades to future multi-gigabit access technologies beyond 10G. Built with a secure-by-design approach, Topaz is designed to support compliance with leading cybersecurity frameworks and regulations, including NIST IR 8425A (U.S.), Radio Equipment Directive (RED), and the Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) (EU).
From a technology differentiation perspective Topaz combines broadband access, packet processing, AI acceleration, advanced security, intelligent power management, and low-latency networking technologies such as L4S and Dual-Queue AQM into a single highly integrated SoC. This integration reduces system complexity, lowers BOM costs, and accelerates product development while enabling differentiated operator services.
The Topaz family provides a scalable portfolio that allows OEMs and operators to optimize system cost and performance for specific applications, ranging from cost-efficient residential gateways to premium multi-gigabit, converged broadband platforms. A common architecture across the family enables extensive hardware and software reuse while preserving flexibility to address diverse market requirements.
Sharing a common software and hardware foundation with MaxLinear's Puma™ 9 DOCSIS® platform, Topaz enables significant code, feature, and development reuse across Cable, Fiber, Ethernet, and FWA product portfolios. This unified platform approach, also known as AnyWAN, shortens software development cycles, simplifies portfolio management, and helps operators rapidly adopt new technologies while reducing engineering investment and long-term support costs.
Platform Architecture & Performance
- Purpose-Built for 10G PON & Beyond: Delivers high-efficiency performance for current 10G deployments while establishing a scalable, long-term architecture for next-generation tiers. High-speed 25G and 50G connectivity, DDR5 memory support, and low latency packet processing are designed to provide long-term headroom for network growth.
- Wi-Fi 8 Ready Infrastructure: Provides the high processing performance, memory bandwidth, and interconnect speeds required to drive deterministic, ultra-low-latency Wi-Fi 8 wireless networks. Topaz handles dense, multi-gigabit traffic across connected home and business environments while minimizing bottlenecks.
- All-in-One High-Integration SoC: Consolidates multi-gigabit fiber access, packet routing, AI/ML acceleration, and advanced security on a single chip. This single-chip design can eliminate the need for separate multi-processor architectures, lowering bill-of-materials (BOM) costs, reducing physical design footprints, and shortening development cycles.
- Low Power Consumption: Features integrated PHYs and Dynamic Power Management (DPM) technology that dynamically scales energy use based on real-time traffic loads. The SoC minimizes power during idle periods while maintaining instant line-rate responsiveness, helping operators meet strict ERP mandates and sustainability goals.
Future-Proof Security & Innovation
- Hardware-Grade Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) Readiness: Optimized for the long deployment lifecycles associated with fiber infrastructure investments, Topaz incorporates advanced hardware-based security technologies and readiness for post-quantum cryptography (PQC). The platform helps operators address emerging cyber threats, evolving security regulations, and requirements such as the European Cyber Resilience Act (CRA).
- Open Ecosystem & Unified Software: Designed around open standards, especially those championed by the prpl Foundation’s prplWare, as well as supporting RDK, Topaz provides maximum application portability. Sharing a common architecture with MaxLinear’s Puma 9 DOCSIS® platform, the device allows operators and OEMs to unify cable and fiber gateway codebases.
- AI & Next-Gen Service Acceleration: Integrates local compute and AI/ML engines to power intelligent edge services allowing both local as well as hybrid solutions together with extended cloud processing. AI-assisted home network diagnostics including preemptive analysis, pre-processed and compressed network statistics as well as AI-enabled security and QoS optimize the operators’ network operations and provide improved customer quality of experience.
- Optimized for Low Latency: The upgraded packet processing engine is optimized to minimize packet delay inside the gateway. The accelerated data path now also includes a hardware-based dual-queue AQM implementation for L4S, bridging the gap between new L4S-enabled services and the network infrastructure.
Executive Quote
“ Operators can’t afford to wait years to upgrade their network infrastructure to meet demands of the AI-driven broadband home,” said Puneet Sethi, Senior Vice President and General Manager, Network Infrastructure and Carrier, at MaxLinear. “ Customers want smart, AI-powered applications for home and business services, but they don’t want to pay a premium for inflated power bills or monthly service fees to make it happen. With Topaz, we are solving for both. Our latest platform not only delivers affordable 10G PON connectivity today, it’s also flexible enough to accelerate operators into the future – without compromising on power efficiency.”
Partner Quotes
“The broadband gateway market continues to demand greater performance, lower power consumption, and faster product development cycles,”said Robert Lin, CEO Askey. “Topaz combines advanced fiber connectivity, AI acceleration, and future-ready networking capabilities within a highly integrated architecture. We believe this platform has the potential to help OEMs deliver innovative gateway solutions while reducing complexity and development costs. We are happy to be early access partner for Topaz and looking forward to incorporating Topaz in our roadmap as industry transitions to AI-enabled broadband services.”
"The convergence of multi-gigabit fiber access, advanced Wi-Fi, and AI-driven services is creating new requirements for broadband gateway platforms,"said James Lee, CEO, Gemtek Technology Co., Ltd. "The Topaz platform is built to provide the processing performance, security, memory bandwidth, and integration needed to support next-generation broadband and Wi-Fi deployments and differentiated operator services. We are excited to work with MaxLinear and leverage Topaz to accelerate innovation for our global customers."
Select OEMs are already designing next-generation gateways with Topaz. By consolidating key broadband, Wi-Fi, security, and processing functions into a single highly integrated platform, Topaz enables operators to deliver superior subscriber experiences while reducing system complexity, lowering power consumption, and improving overall cost efficiency.
MaxLinear will be attending Network X 2026 in Vienna, Austria. Visit us at Booth D21 to see the debut of Topaz, our next-generation PON home gateway platform, and learn how we're enabling the future of broadband connectivity.

articles.title: GC Rieber VivoMega to highlight $20m supply chain expansion at SupplySide Global - Nutraceutical Business Review
articles.summary: GC Rieber VivoMega to highlight $20m supply chain expansion at SupplySide Global  Nutraceutical Business Review
articles.full_text:
Omega-3 concentrate producer GC Rieber VivoMega has announced it will attend this year's SupplySide Global show in Las Vegas, where it will highlight how diversification can create a more resilient future for the ingredient.
The company will be at Booth #4152 from October 28-30.
“[During] our 60-year history, we have seen the omega-3 industry evolve and have continually adapted to meet changing market needs,” said Snorre Glærum Strand, CEO at GC Rieber VivoMega.
"We understand the immediate challenges facing the industry, but we are also looking ahead."
Our experience allows us to respond to the needs of today while continuing to invest in the technology, capacity and solutions that will support the omega-3 category for years to come.
The Norwegian company expanded into the algal omega-3 category back in 2023, launching its portfolio of non-GMO, certified vegan algae oils to provide an alternative to established marine sources of EPA and DHA.
GC Rieber VivoMega said that its broad algal portfolio offers manufacturers additional sourcing and formulation options, but the firm will continue to diversify and expand its omega-3 offerings.
Thus, as part of a long-term approach to supply-chain resilience, the company announced an additional $20m investment, building on the 2024 expansion of its omega-3 manufacturing campus in Norway.
The company did not specify how it would use the funding in its manufacturing operations, but said it would go toward "strengthening production capabilities across both fish and algal omega-3 concentrates."
Snorre explained: “The future of omega-3s isn't just about supply; it’s about building a supply chain resilient enough for a changing world.”
At the SupplySide Global show, GC Rieber VivoMega will also highlight its new partnership with OmegaQuant, an independent, CLIA-certified lab that offers Omega-3 Index testing to researchers, clinicians and the public.
At the company's booth, attendees can participate in free Omega-3 Index testing and receive VivoMega algal omega-3 samples. Participants can test their omega-3 levels before supplementation and again following the sampling period, providing a before-and-after look at changes in their Omega-3 Index.

articles.title: Lithium-Ion Battery Cell Manufacturing Plant Setup in India - IMARC Group
articles.summary: Lithium-Ion Battery Cell Manufacturing Plant Setup in India  IMARC Group
articles.full_text:
Lithium-ion cells are the energy building block of the electric and digital economy. Electric two-wheelers, cars, buses, grid-scale energy storage, telecom towers, inverters, power tools, laptops, and smartphones all depend on them. India still imports almost all of the cells it uses, while demand from electric mobility and renewable energy storage is rising sharply. That gap, together with the Production-Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme for Advanced Chemistry Cells and supportive state policies, makes Lithium-Ion Battery Cell Manufacturing Plant Setup in India one of the most strategic manufacturing opportunities of this decade, though also one of the most capital- and technology-intensive.
Investment depends above all on capacity, measured in gigawatt-hours (GWh), and on the chemistry and cell format chosen. Because nearly all process equipment is automated, precise, and largely imported, and because electrode assembly must happen in dry rooms, the Lithium-Ion Battery Cell Manufacturing Plant Cost is high. It ranges from roughly INR 500 crore for a specialised line below 1 GWh to INR 5,000–7,500 crore for a 5 GWh gigafactory. Cathode materials, graphite, electrolyte, separators, and foils account for most of the operating cost, and energy is the next largest item. Material sourcing, production yield, and scale are therefore the decisions that shape profitability. At stable operations, a well-run plant can deliver a gross margin of 25 to 35% and a net profit margin of 10 to 15%, with payback typically within 5 to 7 years.
This guide is written for investors trying to understand how to start a Lithium-Ion Battery Cell manufacturing plant in India. It covers the main chemistries and cell formats and their markets, the demand outlook, the production process, machinery and raw materials, location and infrastructure, a detailed cost and financial breakdown, the approvals and certifications involved, and how a DPR turns all of this into a bankable plan.
| Key Facts | Details | 
|---|---|
| India Lithium-Ion Battery Market (2025) | USD 3.59 Billion, 11.78% CAGR to 2034 | 
| Projected Market Size (2034) | USD 9.79 Billion | 
| Leading Chemistry | Lithium iron phosphate (LFP), about 30.1% share | 
| Largest Application | Consumer electronics, about 35.2% share | 
| Leading Region | North India, about 33% share | 
| Indicative Total Investment | INR 500–7,500 Crore (sub-1 GWh to 5 GWh) | 
The snapshot shows a fast-growing market in which LFP is gaining ground on safety and cost grounds, consumer electronics remains the largest application, and electric vehicles and energy storage are growing fastest. Domestic cell production is still at an early stage, so almost all demand is currently met by imports. The wide investment range reflects a genuine choice between a focused line making cylindrical or prismatic cells for a specific segment and a multi-GWh gigafactory serving automotive and storage customers. The sections below work through that choice.
Indicative Project Cost in India (2026)
| Parameter | Value | 
|---|---|
| Product Range | LFP and NMC cells in cylindrical, prismatic, or pouch formats | 
| Total Project Investment | INR 500 – 7,500 Crore (capacity-dependent) | 
| Payback Period | 5 – 7 Years | 
| Net Profit Margin | 10 – 15% | 
| IRR | 14 – 20% | 
| Preferred States | Gujarat, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Telangana, Maharashtra, Haryana | 
| Key Approvals | Environmental clearance, SPCB consents, BIS certification, EPR under battery waste rules | 
| Key Requirement | Proven cell technology, dry rooms, and high production yield | 
These ranges provide a realistic frame for early planning, but actual returns depend on chemistry and format, technology partner terms, cathode and lithium prices, production yield during ramp-up, and success in qualifying cells with automotive and storage customers. A site-specific Lithium-Ion Battery Cell Feasibility Report narrows each of these assumptions to your chosen chemistry, format, customers, location, and capacity.
Table of Contents
A lithium-ion cell stores energy by moving lithium ions between a cathode and a graphite anode through a liquid electrolyte, with a thin porous separator keeping the two electrodes apart. Making cells involves three broad stages: electrode manufacturing, in which active materials are mixed into slurries and coated onto aluminium and copper foils; cell assembly, in which electrodes are wound or stacked, placed in a can or pouch, filled with electrolyte, and sealed; and formation and ageing, in which each cell is charged for the first time, conditioned, tested, and graded. Every stage demands tight control of contamination, moisture, and dimensional accuracy, because small defects reduce capacity, cycle life, and safety.
Commercially, cell making is the highest-value step in the battery supply chain. A Lithium-Ion Battery Cell Manufacturing Plant supplies battery pack assemblers for electric two-wheelers, three-wheelers, cars, and buses, energy storage system integrators, telecom and inverter makers, and consumer electronics and power tool brands. Long-term supply agreements with vehicle makers and storage developers underpin volumes, while smaller formats for electronics and tools can provide early revenue as a plant ramps up.
The Main Cell Chemistries and Formats
Choosing the chemistry and cell format is the most important commercial decision, because it determines technology partners, machinery, material supply, and customers:
| Chemistry / Format | Description | Key Property | Primary Demand | 
|---|---|---|---|
| LFP (Lithium Iron Phosphate) | Iron phosphate cathode | Safe, long-life, lower cost | Energy storage, 2W/3W, buses, entry EVs | 
| NMC (Nickel Manganese Cobalt) | Layered nickel-rich cathode | High energy density | Passenger EVs, premium applications | 
| Cylindrical Cells | 18650, 21700, and 4680 formats | Mature, highly automated | 2W, power tools, e-bikes, some EVs | 
| Prismatic Cells | Rectangular aluminium can | Good pack integration | EVs and energy storage | 
| Pouch Cells | Laminated flexible casing | Light and flexible | Electronics and some EVs | 
These choices shape the whole plant. Cylindrical lines run at very high speed with mature, standardised equipment, prismatic lines suit large-format LFP cells for storage and vehicles, and pouch lines need stacking and lamination capability. Many Indian projects start with LFP prismatic or cylindrical cells for two-wheelers, three-wheelers, and energy storage, where demand is strong and the technology is well proven, then add NMC or newer chemistries such as sodium-ion as capacity, partners, and customer approvals grow.
Key Growth Drivers in the Indian Market
Demand is supported by the electrification of transport, the growth of renewable energy, and a strong policy push for domestic manufacturing:
India-Specific Market Opportunity
| Segment | India Market Context | Manufacturing Role | 
|---|---|---|
| Electric Two & Three-Wheelers | Largest EV segment by volume | LFP and NMC cylindrical and prismatic cells | 
| Passenger EVs & Buses | Growing model launches and fleet orders | Large-format prismatic and pouch cells | 
| Energy Storage Systems | Renewable integration and storage tenders | High-cycle LFP prismatic cells | 
| Telecom, UPS & Inverters | Replacement of lead-acid batteries | LFP cells for backup power | 
| Electronics & Power Tools | Large, import-dependent market | Cylindrical and pouch cells | 
The strongest opportunity lies in securing long-term supply agreements with one or two anchor segments, such as electric two-wheelers or energy storage, where Indian demand is large and cells can be standardised. A reliable technology partnership, localisation of cell materials over time, and customer qualification of cells for safety and cycle life are what convert this demand into sustained orders.
Understanding the process helps you plan machinery, dry room area, and where yield and cost are decided. Cell production is a continuous, highly automated sequence from electrode manufacturing through cell assembly to formation and testing. Moisture and particle contamination must be kept to very low levels, so much of the line operates inside dry rooms and clean areas.
The Lithium-Ion Battery Cell Manufacturing Process Flow
The sequence below reflects prismatic and cylindrical cell manufacturing. Pouch lines follow the same electrode steps but use stacking and laminated pouch sealing in place of winding and can assembly.
| Unit Operation | Key Activity | 
|---|---|
| Slurry Mixing | Active materials, binders, and conductive additives mixed | 
| Electrode Coating & Drying | Slurry coated on foils and dried, with solvent recovered | 
| Calendering | Electrodes pressed to precise thickness and density | 
| Slitting & Vacuum Drying | Electrodes cut to width and dried to remove moisture | 
| Winding or Stacking | Cathode, separator, and anode assembled into a cell core | 
| Tab Welding & Casing | Tabs welded and core inserted into can or pouch | 
| Electrolyte Filling & Sealing | Electrolyte injected and cell sealed in a dry room | 
| Formation | First controlled charge and discharge cycles | 
| Ageing & Degassing | Cells rested, monitored, and degassed where needed | 
| Grading, Testing & Packing | Capacity, resistance, and safety checks before dispatch | 
Two factors decide profitability across this flow. The first is yield: scrap rates during ramp-up can be high, and every rejected cell carries the full cost of its materials, so process control, inline inspection, and experienced technical teams matter more than almost anything else. The second is throughput and energy use, because coating, drying, dry rooms, and formation consume large amounts of power, and solvent recovery, heat recovery, and energy-efficient formation equipment with power regeneration reduce operating cost.
The main inputs are cathode active materials such as LFP or NMC, anode graphite, electrolyte, separator film

articles.title: OpenAI has ‘work to do to rebuild trust’ in Australia, executive tells AI inquiry - The Guardian
articles.summary: OpenAI has ‘work to do to rebuild trust’ in Australia, executive tells AI inquiry  The GuardianAustralian Lawmakers Question OpenAI Officials on Breaches  The New York TimesOpenAI’s Jason Kwon gave even-toned, reassuring answers to the Australian government. Did … ChatGPT write this?  The GuardianOpenAI, Anthropic tell Australia they would welcome data breach rules  ReutersOpenAI says its Australian Medicare hack 'not super sophisticated'  Politi...
articles.full_text:
OpenAI has used an appearance before a parliamentary inquiry on AI to apologise again to Australia about the hack on Medicare last month, as media and entertainment organisations argued weakening copyright law for AI model training would leave artists as “roadkill”.
Meanwhile Anthropic told the inquiry it was not seeking to dictate copyright law on model training, but the current rules made it “impossible” to train AI in Australia.
Tuesday morning’s hearing of the joint parliamentary inquiry on artificial intelligence largely focused on copyright licensing for AI training in Australia, amid concerns companies such as Anthropic were pushing the Australian government to adopt an opt-out model, requiring rights holders to specifically opt out of allowing AI to train on their content.
Anthropic’s special envoy, the former US ambassador to Australia Jeffrey Bleich, told the committee that Anthropic had “never tried to dictate to Australia” on copyright.
“We’ve just shared information about how the training works, and then discussed what its implications would be with respect to our capacity to operate here,” he said.
Anthropic suggests current Australian laws mean AI companies need to obtain a licence for the use of every piece of content on the internet as training material. Bleich said this was “technically impossible”.
Anthropic was keen to explore what the Australian government wants to do to incentivise training in Australia, and Bleich said Australia could shape frontier models if they were trained here, otherwise it would ultimately rely on models trained elsewhere.
OpenAI apologised for its AI agents attacking a number of Australian government websites in June. The multibillion-dollar company notified the government via an email to a public-facing address three months after the breach.
“I want to begin with an apology. During internal training and evaluation, our models accessed Australian government websites in ways they were not directed to. That should not have happened. We also should have handled our response better,” OpenAI’s chief strategy officer, Jason Kwon, told the committee on Tuesday afternoon.
“We are sorry, and we know we have work to do to rebuild trust with the Australian people. We are committed to doing that work.”
Following the revelation of a separate hack on the NSW national parks and wildlife service last week, Kwon told the committee OpenAI was reviewing logs of AI agent training dating back to November 2025, which identified the latest hack activity taking place in June.
He promised that should more incidents be identified, government agencies would be notified “very, very quickly”.
OpenAI representatives, while apologetic, downplayed the agent activity on Australian government websites as not “not super sophisticated” compared with the Hugging Face attack. The independent senator David Pocock questioned why the company didn’t contact ministers, instead sending an email “to some arbitrary department email” after the Medicare incident.
“I think that on retrospect, we should have done what you were suggesting … I think people were thinking about this as a technical situation, and they wanted to contact the technical counterparties – but it’s not good enough,” Kwan said.
Anthropic’s head of safeguards, Dave Orr, told the committee the company had reviewed hundreds of millions of transcripts of its models and had not found any cases in which it interacted with Australian government systems in an unauthorised way.
He could not say whether Anthropic’s customers may have used the models on Australian government systems, given the company’s “zero data retention” policy.
‘Artists will become roadkill’
Annabelle Herd, the chief executive of the Australian Recording Industry Association (Aria), told the committee that “Australia’s artists will be the roadkill in the rush” to make deals with AI companies, and said Aria was not against AI frontier model training being done in Australia but it should be done on “our terms”.
“There is nothing less sovereign than rewriting our laws to suit foreign company commercial interests, done the way that big AI is proposing,” she said. “It will devastate the music industry and make Australia a pariah for rights holders globally.”
She said Anthropic and OpenAI were “asking the government for a free ride” and the creative sector was calling on the government not to cave in to their demands.
The ABC told the committee Australia’s existing copyright regime was “completely adequate”.
The ABC’s head of content and legal operations, Kate Gilchrist, said an opt-out system as proposed by AI companies would place burdens and costs on rights holders, as it would require ongoing surveillance to see whether copyright material was being used.
She said for the ABC, it would mean ensuring every site on which the ABC publishes material had opted out.
“We cannot scour the internet and ensure we are opting out on all of those different sites of publication. It simply does not work,” she said.
Gilchrist said she suspected ABC content had been scraped already.
The union representing the entertainment and news sector, the Media Entertainment and Arts Alliance (MEAA), has called for an equitable remuneration scheme that would put fees on companies across the AI technology stack.
“Revenue would support two things: direct payments to creative and media workers whose work contributes to AI systems. And secondly, a cultural fund supporting Australian live entertainment, screen music, public interest journalism and cultural activity,” the MEAA’s acting chief executive, Adam Portelli, said.
The committee is holding hearings from Tuesday to Friday this week.

articles.title: Huawei, Qualcomm Reverse 25-Year Patent Fee Flow - 조선일보
articles.summary: Huawei, Qualcomm Reverse 25-Year Patent Fee Flow  조선일보
articles.full_text:
Chinese tech giant Huawei has signed a patent cross-licensing agreement with U.S. semiconductor company Qualcomm, covering core advanced technologies such as 5G, artificial intelligence (AI), computing, and networking. This marks a reversal for the Chinese company, which previously paid patent fees to U.S. firms but now receives more in royalties than it pays.
Huawei announced on October 5 (local time) that it had finalized a multi-year patent cross-licensing deal with Qualcomm. Under the agreement, both companies will use each other’s patents and pay corresponding fees, with Qualcomm expected to pay Huawei more than Huawei pays Qualcomm. Qualcomm also separately acquired some of Huawei’s AI, computing, and networking patents held in the U.S. The Japanese Nikkei newspaper analyzed, “This marks a de facto reversal of the patent fee flow between the two companies after 25 years, since Huawei first began paying Qualcomm patent fees in 2001.”
The agreement is expected to push Huawei’s cumulative patent licensing revenue beyond 6.9 billion dollars (approximately 9 trillion Korean won). Since 2021, Huawei has earned more from patent licensing than it has paid to other companies, driven by increased royalties from overseas firms, including U.S. companies, in advanced fields like AI. In August, Huawei signed a multi-year patent agreement with U.S. PC maker HP to share Wi-Fi technology.
◇Huawei Increases R&D as US Blocks
Huawei’s expansion in patent licensing coincides with its aggressive R&D investment to achieve technological self-reliance after U.S. sanctions. In 2019, the U.S. added Huawei to an export control list, restricting access to advanced semiconductors and U.S.-origin software and technology.
Huawei responded by aggressively increasing investments in self-developed semiconductors, operating systems (OS), and communication and AI technologies. Its R&D expenditure rose from 131.7 billion Chinese yuan in 2019 to 192.3 billion Chinese yuan (approximately 38 trillion Korean won) last year, a 46% increase. Last year, 21.8% of its total revenue was spent on R&D. During this period, its patent portfolio grew rapidly. In 2025, Huawei filed 7,523 international patent applications, ranking first globally for the ninth consecutive year.
Huawei is also accelerating the development of technologies restricted by U.S. sanctions. Despite being blocked from producing advanced semiconductors via Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), it developed its own smartphone application processor, the Kirin, and resumed global sales of 5G flagship smartphones this year after a five-year hiatus. As U.S. restrictions limited NVIDIA’s sales of advanced AI semiconductors in China, Huawei expanded its own AI accelerator, Ascend, and built its own mobile OS, HarmonyOS, as an alternative to Google’s Android.
◇Expanding Chinese Patent Competitiveness in AI
As U.S.-China technological tensions intensify, not only Huawei but also Chinese R&D investment overall has grown rapidly. China’s R&D expenditure increased by 77%, from approximately 2.21 trillion Chinese yuan in 2019 to 3.93 trillion Chinese yuan last year. This has enabled Chinese companies to license their patents to overseas firms, including U.S. companies, and collect royalties. Chinese telecom equipment maker ZTE won a court ruling in the UK in May, requiring Samsung Electronics to pay 392 million dollars for using its standard-essential patents in mobile communications.
Recently, Chinese technological capabilities have rapidly expanded in AI. According to the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO), Chinese patent applications related to generative AI exceeded 43,000 cases in 2024–2025, the highest globally. Among the top 10 institutions for generative AI patent applications, six were Chinese companies or institutions, including Tencent, Baidu, and the Chinese Academy of Sciences.
However, despite increased R&D and self-developed technologies, experts note that China still faces significant limitations in escaping U.S. technological sanctions. For example, it remains unable to secure extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography equipment, a critical technology for advanced semiconductor production.
A source from the tech industry said, “While China remains under U.S. sanctions in advanced semiconductors, it is rapidly expanding the use of open-weight AI models. With self-developed AI semiconductors now supporting this growth, the gap in AI technology with the U.S. could narrow more quickly in the future.”

articles.title: World Bank Cautious on AI Investment Impact for East Asia’s Economy as Tech Exports Drive Expansion - kaohoon international
articles.summary: World Bank Cautious on AI Investment Impact for East Asia’s Economy as Tech Exports Drive Expansion  kaohoon international
articles.full_text:
The World Bank has revised its 2026 economic growth projection for East Asia and the Pacific upward, attributing the increase primarily to exports linked to artificial intelligence technologies. However, it cautions that the region remains highly susceptible to any reversal in global technology investment trends.
The World Bank’s updated forecast covers 23 economies such as China, Vietnam, Indonesia, Malaysia, and Thailand. According to the recent report released on Tuesday, growth in the region is anticipated to reach 4.5% in 2026—an increase of 0.3 percentage points from the April estimate. The expansion will moderate to 4.4% in 2027 and further to 4.3% in 2028.
Among major economies, Vietnam received the largest upward revision, with growth now anticipated at 7.4%, up by 1.1 percentage points.
Much of the region’s export momentum is concentrated in the AI sector. Outside of AI-related categories, trade performance remained marginal or negative. In most countries, over half of export growth originated from AI-linked goods, with this share surpassing 70% in Malaysia, the Philippines, Thailand, and Vietnam.
South Korea’s official statistics indicated that export value rose dramatically in September to $120.9 billion, largely due to strong semiconductor sales. The World Bank noted that the country’s largest chip companies, Samsung and SK Hynix, together made up 43% of the Kospi index’s market capitalization at the end of April.
On the global stage, the bank commented that AI capital investment has climbed to roughly 6% of U.S. GDP, paralleling the peak during the technology boom of 2000. The current pace of AI investment is more rapid than previous cycles. The Bank for International Settlements has previously observed that the vast scale and speed of the AI surge are reminiscent of past financial bubbles.
The World Bank report also highlighted that much of the financing for AI expansion remains opaque, particularly in private credit markets. It estimates that out of the $2.9 trillion in AI capital spending planned for 2025–2028, $800 billion could come from private credit, a share that grew to 34% of lending activity in 2025 from an 18% five-year average.
Monetary policy tightening is another source of risk; recent interest rate hikes by major central banks—including the first increase by the U.S. Federal Reserve since 2023—could restrain liquidity and investment in the AI sector.
If the AI investment wave moderates, the bank suggests this would not necessarily end the growth cycle, but could indicate investments are currently outpacing realized demand. Historically, a 1% drop in U.S. GDP growth would reduce emerging market expansion by 0.6 percentage points, and would have a greater effect on investments. The region’s extensive role in the AI supply chain means it would be particularly affected by a downturn in AI-related activity.
In Thailand, GDP growth reached an average of 2.4% in 2025 and rose to 2.8% year-on-year during the first quarter of 2026. Nevertheless, expansion eased to 1.9% in the second quarter. Growth was supported primarily by government stimulus, capital spending, and robust export figures, with computers and related components comprising an increasing share of total exports.
Despite these gains, Thailand’s overall manufacturing output contracted, and headline inflation accelerated from negative territory at the start of 2026 to 2.5% in August, primarily because of rising oil prices. Tourist arrivals in the first half of the year dropped to 15.9 million, lower than both the previous year and pre-pandemic levels.
The country also continues to grapple with high levels of public and private debt, as government debt approaches its legal ceiling of 70% of GDP. The bank anticipates growth in Thailand will slow to 2.0% for 2026 and pick up marginally in subsequent years, with elevated inflation and public debt remaining concerns.

articles.title: Italy Approves $3.7 Billion Silicon Box Chip Plant to Strengthen Europe’s Semiconductor Supply Chain- Expert View by Spherical Insights - Spherical Insights
articles.summary: Italy Approves $3.7 Billion Silicon Box Chip Plant to Strengthen Europe’s Semiconductor Supply Chain- Expert View by Spherical Insights  Spherical Insights
articles.full_text:
Italy is backing Silicon Box to strengthen semiconductor capabilities, attract high-tech investment, create jobs, reduce supply-chain vulnerabilities and establish Italy as a strategic European hub for advanced digital manufacturing.
Italy has cleared the financing framework for Silicon Box’s planned semiconductor manufacturing facility in Novara, marking a major step in the country’s strategy to strengthen its position in Europe’s semiconductor industry. The project, known as the Vulcan Project, involves a total investment of €3.2 billion, equivalent to roughly $3.7 billion, with the Italian government providing €1.3 billion (US$1.45 billion) in public support through the semiconductor sector fund established under the European Chips Act.
The project will establish Silicon Box’s first European manufacturing facility and is expected to focus on the back-end stages of semiconductor production, particularly chiplet integration, advanced packaging and testing. According to Italy’s Ministry of Enterprises and Made in Italy, the Novara facility would be the first of its kind in Europe, introducing advanced chiplet and packaging capabilities that are currently not available at this scale within the European Union.

A strategic investment in semiconductor manufacturing
The Silicon Box investment in Novara, Italy, represents a €3.2 billion strategic project aimed at strengthening Europe’s semiconductor supply chain. In October 2026, Italy’s investment agency Invitalia approved €1.3 billion in public support, equivalent to roughly 41% of the total investment. The facility is expected to become Silicon Box’s first European manufacturing site and is projected to create around 1,600 direct jobs at full capacity.
The project focuses on advanced chiplet integration, packaging and testing, technologies increasingly important for artificial intelligence, data centres, electric and autonomous vehicles, telecommunications and high-performance computing. The European Commission granted the facility Open EU Foundry status in March 2026, with full production capacity expected by 2033.
For Italy, the investment supports a broader semiconductor strategy. The country has a multibillion-euro Chips Fund, more than €1 billion committed to EU microelectronics IPCEI projects, and a €225 million (US$252 billion) semiconductor-design centre in Pavia. Italy also ranks second in the EU by number of companies in electronic components and boards.
The project aligns with the EU Chips Act, which aims to mobilise over €100 billion (US$112.1 billion) in policy-driven investment and raise Europe’s semiconductor market share from about 10% to 20% by 2030.
Focus on advanced packaging and chiplets
Silicon Box’s Novara project is significant because it targets the “back-end” of semiconductor production, an area increasingly important as conventional chip scaling becomes more difficult. Instead of producing one large chip, chiplet architecture divides computing functions into smaller components that can be integrated within a single package. This enables manufacturers to combine different technologies and potentially reduce design and production costs.
The technology is particularly relevant to the rapid growth of AI and data-centre computing. The Semiconductor Industry Association estimates that the HBM market alone could reach $21 billion in 2025, reflecting the growing need for advanced memory and packaging solutions in AI systems.
The investment is also notable because Italy identified €4 billion in resources for its national microelectronics strategy, covering investment attraction, research and industrial development. Consequently, Novara could support Europe in developing capabilities beyond traditional wafer fabrication, particularly for AI, high-performance computing and next-generation automotive electronics.
Market Stats
- The Italian semiconductor market was valued at US$5.02 billion in 2025 and is projected to reach approximately US$8.76 billion by 2035, expanding at a CAGR of 5.70%.
- AI market: Italy’s AI market reached €1.8 billion (~$2.0B) in 2025, growing 50% year-on-year.
- AI adoption: 71% of large Italian companies had launched at least one AI project in 2025.
- AI ecosystem: Italy has 1,010 companies offering AI solutions and 135 AI startups funded over the past five years.
- Semiconductor market: Italy’s semiconductor sector is expected to generate approximately $2.3 billion in revenue in 2025, with STMicroelectronics as the dominant national player. Electronic components: Italy’s electronic-components market reached approximately $12.8 billion in 2025, with imports accounting for 68.4% of market size.
- Data centres: Italy had 513 MW of installed data-centre IT capacity in 2024, up 17% year-on-year. More than €10 billion (US$11.2 billion) of investment was expected for 2025-26.
Strengthening Europe’s Semiconductor Supply Chain
Silicon Box’s planned facility in Novara can be viewed as part of Europe’s broader effort to reduce vulnerabilities in a semiconductor industry still heavily concentrated outside the region. The European Commission estimates that East Asia accounts for 56% of global front-end wafer-fabrication capacity, while Europe represents only 9%. More broadly, Europe has around 10% of the global semiconductor market, despite having strong capabilities in research, equipment, automotive and industrial chips.

This imbalance matters because semiconductor disruptions can affect entire manufacturing industries. The European Commission notes that some European countries experienced car-production declines of up to one-third during the 2020-22 chip shortage. At the same time, automotive and industrial applications are particularly important to Europe: automotive chips account for 37% of European semiconductor demand, while industrial applications represent another 28%.
Its importance therefore extends beyond Italy. By adding capacity in a previously limited segment of Europe’s semiconductor value chain, the project could diversify sourcing, strengthen links between chip designers and manufacturers, and support European demand for AI, high-performance computing and electric-vehicle technologies. This complements the EU Chips Act’s target of increasing Europe’s global semiconductor share from 10% to 20% by 2030.
Why Italy is backing the investment
The primary purpose of the investment is to strengthen Italy’s domestic semiconductor capabilities, attract high-tech manufacturing, reduce vulnerabilities in critical supply chains and support Europe’s technological independence.
Italy is also seeking to position itself as a production platform for the wider digital economy. Italian Industry Minister Adolfo Urso described the project as reinforcing the country's role as a productive platform for the digital economy.
The government has also designated Silicon Box's investment as a project of strategic national interest. Italy has developed mechanisms to accelerate major strategic investments, particularly those involving foreign companies and technologies considered important to national industrial competitiveness.
For Silicon Box, establishing a European manufacturing base provides access to one of the world's largest industrial markets while allowing the company to develop advanced packaging capabilities closer to European customers.
Italy’s Government AI Policy
Italy has developed a national AI policy focused on innovation, competitiveness and responsible use. Its Italian Strategy for Artificial Intelligence 2024-2026 concentrates on four areas: research, public administration, businesses and education/training. The strategy aims to strengthen domestic AI research, encourage companies to adopt AI and improve government services through digital technologies.
In September 2025, Italy approved its national AI law, establishing a framework aligned with the EU AI Act. The legislation emphasises human oversight, transparency, cybersecurity, privacy and accountability, with rules covering healthcare, employment, education, justice and public administration. AgID and the National Cybersecurity Agency (ACN) were designated as key national AI authorities.
A major economic component is a €1 billion (US$1.12 billion) investment programme supporting AI, cybersecurity and related emerging technologies, particularly startups and SMEs. Digital Transformation Department
Overall, Italy’s approach combines regulation with industrial policy, seeking to develop domestic AI capabilities while ensuring that adoption remains secure, transparent and human-centred. This policy direction also complements Italy’s wider investment in semiconductors, digital infrastructure and advanced technologies.
Opportunities for equipment and technology suppliers
- Strong packaging demand: Global assembly and packaging equipment sales grew 21% in 2025, while test-equipment billings increased by 55%, driven partly by AI-related demand.
- Automation opportunities: The facility’s advanced manufacturing model could generate demand for industrial robots, automated material handling, process-control systems and precision manufacturing equipment.

- Cleanroom infrastructure: Suppliers could benefit from demand for cleanroom systems, temperature and humidity controls, power management and specialised facility infrastructure.

articles.full_text:
Coffee prices today, October 5, 2026
 World coffee prices rose across the board last week.
 Over the past week, robusta coffee futures contracts for November 2026 delivery on the London exchange rose 3% ($102/ton) to $3,469/ton. The January 2027 contract increased 3.2% ($106/ton) to $3,448/ton.
 Meanwhile, the price of Arabica coffee on the New York exchange for March 2027 delivery also increased by 3.4% (9.3 US cents/pound), reaching 280.5 US cents/pound. The May 2027 contract increased by 3.3% (8.9 US cents/pound), reaching 277.8 US cents/pound.
 Traders say the recent recovery is mainly due to short covering. Data released by the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) shows that in the week ending September 29, speculators reduced their short positions in arabica coffee futures on the ICE US exchange. Accordingly, net short positions in arabica coffee decreased by 2,978 contracts, to 3,493 contracts.
 The upward trend last week was also due to the fact that most of the old crop's inventory had been depleted, while the new crop's supply is still a few weeks away from appearing.
 Meanwhile, the market is closely monitoring weather developments in Brazil as well as factors that could impact global coffee supply. Regular rainfall in Brazil is crucial for coffee flowering. However, the most unpredictable factor currently is El Niño, which is predicted to be one of the strongest El Niño events ever recorded. El Niño can cause adverse weather patterns such as floods, droughts, and temperature fluctuations, thereby negatively impacting coffee production, particularly in Asia, Central America, and South America.
 The Climate Prediction Center of the U.S. National Weather Service forecasts a 75% chance that El Niño will continue until early 2027. The intensity and timing of El Niño will determine the extent of its impact on coffee production.
 On September 30th, certified arabica coffee inventories at New York exchange warehouses decreased by 290 bags, to 260,364 bags. At the same time last year, inventories were more than double the current level. Since the beginning of the year, inventories have decreased by over 40%. For robusta coffee, certified inventories at the London exchange decreased by 32,000 bags, to 864,000 bags.
 Domestic coffee prices also increased slightly last week, fluctuating around 94,000 VND/ounce. Although they edged up, the increase in domestic coffee prices was still significantly lower than in the international market.
 The Vietnamese coffee market remained generally quiet this week due to the depletion of existing coffee stocks from the previous harvest, while new coffee supplies are still a few weeks away. However, traders reported that domestic green coffee prices have edged up.
 Vietnam officially begins its new coffee crop season this Thursday, but traders say it's unlikely that large quantities of the new crop will be available on the market before early November. Traders say the price of the upcoming harvest remains uncertain and difficult to predict. Prices will depend on several factors, including developments in Brazil and weather conditions in the Central Highlands of Vietnam next month. However, current conditions are favorable for coffee cultivation.
 According to data released by the Vietnam General Statistics Office, Vietnam exported 1.45 million tons of coffee in the first nine months of 2026, a 16.2% increase compared to the same period last year. However, the export value of coffee during this period decreased by 7%, to $6.6 billion. In September alone, Vietnam exported 124,000 tons of coffee, a 53% increase compared to the same period last year.
